title: Making Introductions
short: Say the honored person's name first: an older person, a guest, a client, or a senior colleague; at work, rank decides, not age or gender.
trouble: Learners avoid introducing people because they fear the order. Saying the names warmly matters far more than the order; a forgotten introduction is the real slip.

blocks.html: You already know how to introduce two people: say the older person's name first and give each a detail to talk about. Adult life adds new settings, such as work, clients and formal events, but the same idea runs through all of them.

Say the honored person's name first, then present the other person to them: an older person, a guest, a client, or a senior colleague. At work, rank decides, not age or gender. Then add a detail so they can start talking.

Saying someone's name first is a small gesture of respect, like holding a door. It tells the honored person, "I am bringing this person to meet you." The added detail does the real work of an introduction: it gives two strangers something to say, so the introducer can step back and the conversation can begin.

head: Say this name first
When you introduce them to
rows: A guest or newcomer at a family event
Anyone from your own company, even your boss
An official or someone with a title

blocks.name: et-intro

details: Mr. Mensah runs the bakery chain we are working with.

blocks.cap: At work, the client is honored, even above your own manager.

blocks.title: A family visit
blocks.q: Leo brings his new friend Sam home and meets his grandmother, Mrs. Hale. What does Leo say?
steps: Mrs. Hale is older, so her name comes first.
"Grandma, this is my friend Sam Rivera. Sam, this is my grandmother, Mrs. Hale."
He adds a detail: "Sam and I are on the robotics team."
blocks.a: Grandmother's name first, then Sam's, then a detail.

blocks.title: Rank at work
blocks.q: Nora, a junior analyst, introduces James, a vice president of her company, to Ruby, a new intern. Whose name comes first?
steps: James is senior, so his name comes first: "James, I'd like you to meet Ruby Walsh, our new intern. Ruby, this is James Reed, our vice president."

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: Introducing two people
items: Say "I'd like you to meet…" and the other person's full name
Turn and say the honored person's name to the other
Let them talk, and step back

blocks.cap: Put the steps of an introduction in order.

blocks.html: Avoiding introductions because you fear getting the order wrong. Saying the names warmly matters far more than the order; a forgotten introduction, leaving someone standing unnamed, is the real slip. If you mix up the order, keep going: nobody will mind.

sources.name: Present-day American custom, as etiquette writers widely describe it: the order of introductions

Emily Post, Etiquette in Society, in Business, in Politics and at Home (1922; public domain), its chapter on introductions (history; the rule that a man is always presented to a woman has given way to rank and age)
